subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 1 of Year 4 Computing at Ehel Academy. You learn how a computer can make a character move by repeating instructions, and use that idea to build simple animations in Scratch. The big new idea is repetition — doing something over and over — and the tool for repetition in Scratch is the Forever block. An animation is just a set of pictures shown one after another, fast, so it looks like movement. When you make a butterfly flap its wings forever, they are watching a loop happen before their eyes. First, to follow, understand and correct algorithms that use repetition — to read steps, spot where they repeat, and fix them if they are wrong. Second, to add comments to your code — short notes that explain what it does, like a label on a jar. Third, to develop programs with repetition in Scratch using the Forever block, so a character repeats an action without stopping.

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 4 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: These objectives come straight from the source unit. By the end, the child should be able to:
Follow, understand and correct algorithms that use repetition — read steps that repeat, say what job they do, and fix them when a step is wrong.
Understand what a forever loop is — instructions that repeat over and over without stopping.
Add comments to blocks of code to explain what the code does.
Develop programs with repetition in Scratch using the Forever block.
Build a simple animation by switching costumes and moving a sprite inside a forever loop.

Before starting, it helps if the child already knows what an algorithm is (a set of steps in the right order) and has changed a block of code before. A quick reminder in Session 1 is enough — do not spend a whole session revising.

concepts.title: What is repetition? Loops all around us (unplugged)
concepts.explanation: Repetition means doing something over and over. Loops are all around us — many things in the world repeat again and again. In computing, we use repetition to make a character repeat an action, and that is how animation works. How did you know what to do next? Doing something over and over is called repetition. Start with a clapping game.
concepts.example: Answer this in your own words, out loud or on paper: What is repetition? Loops all around us? Then check your answer against the explanation above.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you point to the part of a pattern that repeats, and give an example of a real-life loop?

concepts.title: Forever loops in algorithms (unplugged)
concepts.explanation:
A forever loop is repetition where the instructions repeat over and over without stopping. Instead of writing the same step again and again, we write it once and say “repeat forever”. March on the spot, forever. That is a forever loop.

Try it: Ask you to follow the steps out loud first, then fill the gaps.

Check yourself: Can you replace a repeated step with “repeat forever” instead of copying it many times? Do you understand that a forever loop repeats until you stop it? Praise anyone who notices the forever version is shorter but does more.
concepts.example: I gave the instruction once, and it repeated until I stopped it. I did not have to keep saying it.

concepts.title: Your first animation in Scratch (the Forever block)
concepts.explanation:
In Scratch we join coloured blocks to make a program. To repeat blocks over and over, we drop them inside the Forever block, in the Control group. Everything inside it repeats until we stop the program. We will use it to make a butterfly flap forever.

concepts.title: Adding comments, and a walking chick
concepts.explanation: A comment is a note we add to our code to explain what it does. Comments help other people (and our future selves) understand the program, and help with debugging — finding and fixing mistakes. Unlike the rest of the code, a comment does not run. We will also make a chick that walks and changes costume forever. The label does not change what is inside — it just reminds us. A comment is like a label for our code. Right-click a block. Choose Add Comment.

concepts.title: Animating a moving character (and adding sound)
concepts.explanation: We put together everything we know — repetition, the Forever block, moving, switching costumes, and comments — to animate a character that moves side to side, and we add a sound. Add the Ballerina sprite (a built-in Scratch character) and the Theater 2 backdrop. We want the character to sway right, then back left, over and over.

debugging.symptom: A forever loop just means do it a lot of times.
debugging.cause: A common mix-up in this unit, “Be an Animator”.
debugging.fix: No — it means do it over and over with no end, until you press stop. Show the butterfly flapping and you can see it never stops on its own.

debugging.symptom: I need to copy the blocks many times to repeat them.
debugging.cause: A common mix-up in this unit, “Be an Animator”.
debugging.fix: This is the whole reason the Forever block exists — one Forever block does the job of many copied blocks, and is far tidier.

debugging.symptom: You can put blocks after a Forever block.
debugging.cause: A common mix-up in this unit, “Be an Animator”.
debugging.fix: Nothing below a Forever block ever runs, because the loop never ends. Scratch will not even let a block snap on below it.

debugging.symptom: Comments make the program work / comments run like code.
debugging.cause: A common mix-up in this unit, “Be an Animator”.
debugging.fix: Comments never run. Prove it by running the program with and without a comment — it behaves the same.

selfAssessment: I can these objectives come straight from the source unit. By the end, the child should be able to:
I can follow, understand and correct algorithms that use repetition — read steps that repeat, say what job they do, and fix them when a step is wrong.
I can understand what a forever loop is — instructions that repeat over and over without stopping.
I can add comments to blocks of code to explain what the code does.
I can develop programs with repetition in Scratch using the Forever block.
I can build a simple animation by switching costumes and moving a sprite inside a forever loop.

I can before starting, it helps if the child already knows what an algorithm is (a set of steps in the right order) and has changed a block of code before. A quick reminder in Session 1 is enough — do not spend a whole session revising.
